title: Unpack a hard sentence by fixed questions
statement: Teach learners to unpack a hard sentence by fixed questions: who or what, doing what, to whom, and why that word.
detail: A reading course's review standard, citing an IES video on scaffolding emergent reading for dual-language learners, has a hard sentence unpacked by a scripted routine that names its connectives and that-phrases and chunks it physically, rather than only flagging it as hard (`grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/skills/g3-reading-red-team/references/dimensions/D8-text-quality.md`, lines 26-27). A second IES video, on foundational reading skills, supplies the cohesion devices to teach by name: pronoun referents, connectives, substitution, repetition and ellipsis, nominalisation and deixis. A reader who can decode every word can still lose the thread in one long sentence, and naming each device makes it teachable.

evidence.quote: Troublemaker sentences are unpacked with a scripted routine that names connectives/that-phrases and physically chunks the sentence (who/what → doing → to whom → why that word), not just flagged
Cohesion instruction covers the specific devices — pronoun referents, connectives, substitution, repetition/ellipsis, nominalization ('this question' pointing back), deixis (me/here), analogies
a Grade-3 reader who can decode every word can still drown in one long sentence full of subordinate clauses, connectives, and a "she" three lines back
